lines.text: A microwave heats your food in two minutes, but the plate stays cool. How does it pick what to heat?
Inside, a tube called a magnetron makes microwaves. The same kind of radio wave as Wi-Fi, at about two point four five gigahertz.
Food is full of water. And each water molecule has a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, like a tiny magnet.
The microwave's field flips back and forth billions of times a second. The water molecules try to follow, spinning back and forth.
All that jostling and bumping is heat. The food warms itself from the water inside.
Most plates and glass have almost no free water, so the waves pass right through them. That's why the plate stays cooler.
But the waves bounce around the metal box and make hot and cold spots. That's why the plate spins, and why you stir.
And the dots on the door? That metal mesh has holes far smaller than the waves, so they can't get out. But light can, so you can watch.
Keep it in the box. That's Orbi Transfer's private Space: only people with the passcode get in, and nobody outside even sees it.
